section.title: Titus and the Delegation
section.sectionRationale: Having appealed for the collection on the ground of grace and the example of Christ, Paul now attends to the practical integrity of the work. He is sending Titus and two trusted brothers ahead so that the large sum may be handled above reproach, and so that the Corinthians will be ready when he arrives. The passage shows the care Paul takes to guard his ministry from any hint of scandal and to secure a gift given willingly rather than grudgingly.
section.thesis: Because the handling of the churches' generosity must be honorable in the eyes of both God and men, Paul commissions a trusted delegation to oversee the collection and to prepare the Corinthians in advance, so that their gift may be ready as a genuine act of blessing and the confidence he has expressed in them may not prove empty.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the sending of Titus and the brothers whom God has stirred and the churches have chosen; the safeguard of doing what is right before God and men, with the messengers who are the glory of Christ; and the advance arrangements so the Corinthians will be ready and the boasting not be found empty.

units.label: Titus and the brothers are sent
units.note: the same devotion put into Titus's heart

verses.text: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same {{spoude|devotion}} I have for you.
For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition.
Along with Titus we are sending the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel.
More than that, this brother was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the gracious offering we administer to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help.

units.label: Doing what is right before God and men
units.note: the messengers, the glory of Christ

verses.text: We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift.
For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men.
And we are sending along with them our brother who has proven his earnestness to us many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you.
As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the {{doxa|glory}} of Christ.
In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you.

units.label: Ready, so the boast is not empty
units.note: a generous gift prepared, not begrudged

verses.text: Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you.
For I know your eagerness to help, and I have been boasting to the Macedonians that since last year you in Achaia were prepared to give. And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise.
But I am sending the brothers in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said.
Otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we, to say nothing of you, would be ashamed of having been so confident.

So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to visit you beforehand and make arrangements for the generous gift you had promised. This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly.

spoude.gloss: Diligence, earnestness, eager devotion, haste in a good sense. Paul thanks God for putting into the heart of Titus the same spoude, the same earnest care, that Paul himself has for the Corinthians. The word describes a wholehearted zeal that does not drag its feet but presses eagerly toward the good work. It marks the whole delegation, who are commended repeatedly for their proven earnestness in the service of the gospel.

doxa.gloss: Glory, honor, radiance, the visible display of worth. Paul calls the brothers who carry the collection the glory of Christ, meaning that in their faithful service the honor and radiance of Christ are put on display. Their integrity and love reflect the character of their Lord, so that as they minister among the churches, it is Christ who is seen and magnified through them.

basic.context: Paul turns from the theology of giving to its careful administration. He is sending Titus, who shares Paul's own eager care for the Corinthians, along with two trusted brothers chosen by the churches, to complete the collection. He is determined that so large a sum be handled honorably before both God and men, and that the Corinthians be ready when he and possibly some Macedonians arrive, so the confidence he has voiced about them proves true.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not dull logistics but a window into ministry integrity. Paul's insistence on doing what is right in the eyes of men as well as the Lord teaches that transparent handling of money is a gospel matter. Read the delegation and the advance arrangements as a model of accountability that protects both the mission and the giver.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul thanks God for the spoude, the eager devotion, that God placed in Titus's heart, the same earnestness Paul has for the church. He calls the brothers who carry the gift the doxa, the glory, of Christ, so that in their faithful service the honor of Christ is displayed.
basic.typology: The brothers who carry the offering to Jerusalem, tested and trusted, stand in the line of faithful stewards throughout Scripture whose reliability reflects a greater Steward. Their transparent service anticipates the perfect faithfulness of Christ, who handled all that the Father gave Him without loss.
basic.christ: The brothers are called the glory of Christ, for in their integrity and love the character of the Lord shines out. Christ is the one whose own faithful stewardship of the Father's will they reflect, and it is His honor, not their own, that their labor is meant to display and magnify among the churches.
basic.god: It is God who put the eager devotion into Titus's heart, showing that even the willing servants of a good work are His gift. Paul's concern to do right before both God and men reflects a God who sees in secret yet also cares that His name be honored openly, so that the watching world sees the integrity of His people.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12 urges zeal that is not slothful in serving the Lord. 1 Corinthians 16 arranges for approved men to carry the gift to Jerusalem. Proverbs 3 speaks of finding favor in the sight of God and man. 1 Peter 2 calls believers to keep their conduct honorable among the nations.
basic.oneStory: The gospel produces not only generous hearts but honest hands. As God's people share their resources across the world, He raises up faithful stewards whose integrity displays the glory of Christ, so that the ministry of giving is guarded from scandal and the name of the Lord is honored before a watching world.

context.literary:
The section is built from three small portraits and one warning. Titus is introduced in verses 16 and 17, the first unnamed brother in verses 18 and 19, the second in verse 22, and then verse 23 sums all three up in two matching sentences, 'As for Titus... As for our brothers...' The pairing gives Titus a place as Paul's own partner and the others a place as the churches' representatives. Verse 24 turns from the messengers to the Corinthians: show them proof of your love. The chapter division then interrupts, but the thought carries straight on into chapter 9.

Chapter 9 begins with a puzzle that has long interested readers. Verse 1 says there is no need to write about the service to the saints, and then Paul writes about it for another fourteen verses. The effect is a piece of tactful rhetoric called praeteritio, saying one need not speak of something while speaking of it. It lets Paul say what he must without seeming to doubt them. His boasting in 9:2 is both a compliment and a pressure, and 9:3 to 5 make that pressure explicit with the word 'ashamed.'

The language is full of repetition. Spoude, earnestness, recurs in the section, eagerness and zeal in 9:2, and the word for boasting returns in 8:24, 9:2 and 9:3. The repeated key words bind a list of arrangements into a single argument, that a gift is a matter of character on both sides, the giver's and the carrier's. The movement ends with a contrast of two words in 9:5, blessing and greed, which prepares the reader for the great teaching on generosity that follows in 9:6.
context.historical:
Moving money across the Roman Mediterranean was dangerous. Roads and sea lanes had their robbers, and a large sum collected from many churches would have been an obvious temptation. It was also a matter of reputation. Itinerant teachers in Corinth were known for taking payment, and Paul's critics had already suggested he would profit from his work. In 12:16 he reports that some had said he caught them by trickery, and he meets that charge directly in 12:17-18 by asking whether Titus or any of the others had taken advantage of them. The delegation's careful make-up is Paul's answer to that suspicion long before it is voiced.

The system itself was shrewd. The churches choose their own representative, verse 19, and in 1 Corinthians 16:3-4 the Corinthians are told they may do the same, with letters of recommendation. Because the delegates were chosen by the donors and not simply by Paul, no one could say he had handpicked his friends to carry the money. Acts 20:4 gives us a glimpse of the actual party that later traveled with Paul, drawn from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and Asia, a cross-section of the churches that gave.

Honor and shame were powerful forces. To have boasted publicly that Achaia was ready and then to arrive with Macedonian visitors to find an empty purse would have been a public humiliation for everyone. Paul's frank mention of shame in 9:4 would have been understood in just those terms. He is not trying to manipulate them. He is naming the real social stakes in a culture where reputation was a form of currency, and then offering them the means to avoid it, namely preparation beforehand, verse 5.
context.canonical:
The principle that ministry should be above reproach stands behind the qualifications for church leaders. An overseer must not be greedy for gain and must have a good reputation with outsiders, 1 Timothy 3:3 and 3:7, and Peter tells elders to shepherd the flock not for shameful gain but eagerly, 1 Peter 5:2. Paul's own refusal of support in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 9:12 and 2 Corinthians 11:7-9, comes from the same concern, and so does his reminder to the Thessalonians that he never used a pretext for greed, 1 Thessalonians 2:5.

The phrase in verse 21 echoes Proverbs 3:4, in the Greek translation, and is quoted in Romans 12:17: 'Be careful to do what is right in the eyes of everyone.' The Old Testament teaching on honest weights and measures, Proverbs 11:1, and the story of the generous freewill gifts for the tabernacle that were overseen by honest men, Exodus 38:21-23, belong to the same family.

Paul's name for the delegates, apostoloi of the churches, adds a note about the word 'apostle.' It means one who is sent, and in the New Testament it is used of the Twelve and Paul in a unique sense and of other commissioned messengers, such as Epaphroditus in Philippians 2:25, in a lesser one. The chapter also anticipates the work of the deacons in Acts 6:1-6, where honest and Spirit-filled men are chosen to manage the distribution of funds. In each case the church's money is treated as sacred trust.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote this section for two audiences at once. To the Corinthians he is saying that the collection will be handled by people they can trust and that he is counting on them to be ready. To any who still suspected his motives he was giving evidence in advance. Almost every phrase serves one of these aims.

He wanted the Corinthians to receive Titus gladly. Titus had brought Paul good news about their repentance, 7:6 and 7:13-15, and Paul needs the church to see his return as a partnership and not a rebuke. That is why verses 16 and 17 stress Titus's own eagerness and his own choice to come.

He also wanted them to see the delegation as a proof of love, verse 24. The churches had sent men, and they were watching how Corinth treated them. A warm welcome and a ready gift would show that the Corinthians were part of the same family.

Last, Paul wanted to make the promise real. His boasting in Macedonia had created expectations. By sending the brothers ahead he gave the Corinthians a gracious opportunity to be what he had said they were, rather than be shamed. The whole passage reflects a pastor's firm kindness: he trusts them, he tells them so, and he arranges matters so that their trust in him and in God is rewarded.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The names and routes of the delegation are descriptive, a record of a particular trip with particular people. Paul does not command every church to appoint three delegates or to travel in advance of the collection. The unnamed brothers cannot be turned into a template for church staffing.

What the passage prescribes is a set of principles. People who handle money for the sake of the gospel should be tested and trusted, as the second brother was, verse 22. They should be chosen by those whose money it is, verse 19. Their work should be open to scrutiny so that no one can raise a fair complaint, verse 20. A church that makes a promise should keep it and should prepare ahead rather than be rushed at the last moment, verse 5. And leaders should care about the reputation of the gospel in the eyes of people outside as well as God's own judgment, verse 21.

The passage does not say that Christians must disclose every personal financial detail to everyone. It says that those entrusted with the gifts of others must act in a way that answers honest questions and cannot be fairly accused. Churches and ministries today can take that seriously through audited accounts, plural oversight and clear reporting, without inventing a rule that the text does not give.

debates.question: Who are the two unnamed brothers of 8:18 and 8:22?

views.label: Deliberately unnamed because their character was the credential
views.case: Paul describes them by reputation and by the churches' choice and not by name. The first is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel, and the second has been tested often. If Titus carried the letter, he could name them aloud. The omission fits Paul's emphasis that their value lies in their proven character.

views.label: Known co-workers, such as Luke or Trophimus and Tychicus
views.case: Since the early centuries readers have suggested names, with Luke often proposed for the brother famed for the gospel, or others from Acts 20:4. The suggestions rest on guesses about the associations of Paul's companions, and the text supplies no names.

views.label: Representatives of the Macedonian churches
views.case: Verse 19 says one was chosen by the churches, which many take to mean the Macedonian churches that Paul had just praised. This would suit the strong theme of Macedonian participation, and it would suggest that Macedonian eyes were on Corinth.

debates.bearing: We cannot name them with confidence, and Paul did not need to. What matters is that each was vouched for by those who knew him, which is precisely the kind of testimony that makes a person fit to carry other people's gifts.

debates.question: Is Paul being manipulative in his appeal to boasting and shame in 9:1 to 5?

views.label: A fair appeal to promises made
views.case: The Corinthians had pledged a year earlier and Paul had told the Macedonians so. Reminding them of that is reminding them of their own word. He does not threaten, and he gives the means to succeed, which is advance preparation.

views.label: Pressure that sits uneasily with grace
views.case: Others feel that a gift prompted by fear of embarrassment hardly matches the freedom that chapter 9 teaches, and that Paul is uncomfortably close to coercion. Verse 5 speaks of their gift as not begrudging, and this critique asks whether pressure can make a free gift.

views.label: Honor and shame as ordinary moral language
views.case: In the world of the letter, honor and shame were a natural way to talk about keeping faith. Paul uses the vocabulary of his culture but turns it toward God's grace by repeatedly naming the gift a blessing, 9:5, and a service, 9:12.

debates.bearing: Paul is open about the stakes and clear that the gift must be willing. The next verses go on to say that each should give as he has decided in his heart, not under compulsion, 9:7, which shows that Paul himself did not want a gift extracted by embarrassment.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with spoude in verses 16, 17 and 22. The word suggests haste as well as earnestness, a readiness to move. In verse 17 Titus is said to be going of his own accord, authairetos, the same self-chosen willingness that Paul praised in the Macedonians in 8:3. Paul says in the same verse that he welcomed the appeal. The word parakaleo, urge, ties Titus's consent to the larger theme of Paul's appeals through these chapters. So Titus does not go as a mere agent. He goes as a partner who shares the apostle's heart.

Verse 19 says the second man was 'chosen' by the churches. The verb is cheirotoneo, which originally meant to appoint by a show of hands. It is used in Acts 14:23 for the appointing of elders. The choice is a public, communal act, and Paul gives it weight. He also calls the offering a charis, a gracious work, which the delegates 'administer,' diakoneo. The language of service and grace belongs to the carriers as well as the gift.

In verse 20 Paul says he wants to 'avoid,' and the Greek verb, stellomai, means to take precautions or to steer clear. The thing avoided is momos, 'blame' or 'fault-finding.' The related noun means a blemish. He is arranging things so that no stain can fairly be fixed on his handling of the gift. Verse 21 says he takes great care, pronoeo, 'to provide ahead' for what is honorable in the eyes of both the Lord and people. The same expression is used in Romans 12:17, where it is a duty laid on all believers.

Verse 23 contains two nouns that deserve notice. Titus is koinonos, partner, and synergos, fellow worker. The delegates are apostoloi ekklesion, messengers or apostles of the churches. The English 'messengers' hides the word apostle, but the footnote shows that 'apostles' is a possible rendering. In Paul's usage the word covers those sent by a church as well as those sent by Christ. The final phrase, doxa Christou, 'the glory of Christ,' is a sharp description. They are not themselves the glory, but they reflect it.

In 9:1 Paul says it is 'superfluous' to write, using the word perisson. In 9:3 he fears his boasting will be proved 'empty,' kenoo, the verb of emptying that appears in Philippians 2:7 of Christ emptying Himself. The word for 'confident' in 9:4 is hypostasis, a word of firm foundation, used in Hebrews 11:1 for the assurance of faith. The chapter ends its first movement with a pair of contrasts in 9:5: eulogia, 'blessing,' which the BSB renders 'generous gift,' and pleonexia, 'greed' or 'grasping,' translated 'begrudgingly.' The offering will be either a blessing given or a thing extorted, and the choice depends on whether the heart is ready.

typology.type: The overseers of the tabernacle offering, Exodus 38:21-23
typology.fulfillment: When the gifts for the tabernacle were counted, the work was entrusted to named men under Moses' direction and the accounts were set down openly. The pattern shows that sacred gifts are to be handled openly and by those who can be trusted. Paul's delegation is a New Testament form of the same care. In Christ the sanctuary becomes His people, so that the collection is a gift to living saints. The type falls short in that the tabernacle accounts were kept for a building, whereas these messengers carry relief to a family.

typology.type: The seven men chosen to serve tables, Acts 6:1-6
typology.fulfillment: The Jerusalem church picked seven men known to be full of the Spirit and of wisdom to oversee the daily distribution, and the whole community approved. Paul's delegation repeats the shape: trusted men, chosen by the community, to handle shared resources. This continuity shows that the ministry of care for the poor was always meant to be public and accountable. The pattern points to Christ, who served others without reserve, Mark 10:45. It falls short in that the Seven served within one city, while these delegates tie together churches across a whole region.

typology.type: Titus and the brothers as sent ones, Luke 10:1-3
typology.fulfillment: Jesus sent out the seventy-two in pairs ahead of Him to every place He was about to visit. Titus and the two brothers go ahead of Paul to prepare Corinth for his coming, as the seventy-two prepared towns for the Lord. They are not the master, but they prepare the way for him. The escalation is that the sent ones now carry out the Lord's own work after His ascension. The correspondence is real but loose, since Paul does not himself cite the Luke passage, and the comparison should be held lightly.

typology.type: The glory of Christ displayed in His servants, Exodus 34:29-35
typology.fulfillment: When Moses came down the mountain his face shone because he had spoken with the LORD, and the people could see that he had been in God's presence. In 2 Corinthians 3:7-18 Paul has already compared the two ministries, and in 3:18 believers behold the glory of the Lord and are changed. The delegates called the glory of Christ are a modest but real instance of that change. The greater glory is Christ Himself. The type falls short because Moses' radiance faded, while the glory in Christ's people is the glory of one whose life does not end.

study.christ:
The Lord appears in this passage by name only twice, in 'the glory of Christ' and in 'the eyes of the Lord,' but He is present throughout as the one whose character the messengers imitate. A section of Paul's letter that might seem merely administrative turns out to belong to the gospel.

Take the phrase in verse 23, doxa Christou. In the Bible's own vocabulary, glory is the weight and radiance of God. Christ is called the radiance of God's glory in Hebrews 1:3, and in John 1:14 the disciples beheld His glory as the only Son of the Father. To call three working men the glory of Christ is a bold thing to say. It means that their honest handling of money, their willingness to travel and their tested love are the kind of thing that makes the Lord visible. They are lamps lit from Him.

The movement of the whole collection is also christological. It is made possible by the pattern of 8:9, where the Lord who was rich became poor. The brothers are carrying a gift from people who have learned that pattern to people in need. Their journey from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem is a small reflection of the Son's journey from heaven to earth, bearing a gift that costs the giver.

There is another link in the quality Paul asks of them. Christ was faithful in all that was given Him. Hebrews 3:2 says that He was faithful to the One who appointed Him, and in John 17:12 He says that He lost none of those the Father had given Him. The stewards of this gift are a reflection of the faithful steward. It matters that they are called to be above reproach before the world, for Christ Himself, Peter says, left an example that did no wrong, 1 Peter 2:21-22.

Finally, the unity the collection expresses is Christ's own work. Ephesians 2:14-16 says that He is our peace, who has made the two groups one and broken down the dividing wall. A Gentile church sending relief to a Jewish church is that peace made visible. Christ is the reason the delegates are traveling at all. He has made one family out of the nations and Israel, and the delegates are carrying the family's love from one house of it to another. Anyone who treats them well is, in the sense of Matthew 25:40, treating the Lord well.
study.god:
This section does not speak of God as often as chapter 8 does, but its small remarks about Him are precise. The first is a thanksgiving: 'thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion.' Paul does not treat Titus's zeal as a credit to Titus or to himself. It is a gift. The Lord who moves hearts is the God who sets the whole plan in motion, and He does so through ordinary people who really act of their own accord. Paul sees no conflict between 'God put it into his heart' and 'he is going of his own volition,' both said within two verses. That is a striking picture of divine and human action held together.

The second is that the work is done to honor the Lord Himself, verse 19. The collection is not primarily a fundraising campaign. It is a service of worship aimed at God. Everything else, the delegation, the accountability and the advance preparation, is arranged for that purpose.

The third is the reach of His sight. Paul takes great care to do what is right 'not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men.' The first half assumes a God who sees what no auditor can see, Proverbs 15:3. Yet the second half shows that the God who sees in secret also cares about public credibility, because His name is attached to His people. The honor of God is at stake in how the church handles a purse.

The fourth is His character as the one who loves integrity. Throughout Scripture He is the God of honest weights, Proverbs 11:1, and of a people called to be blameless, Philippians 2:15. A church that is careless about money is careless about the truth of the God it claims to represent.

Finally, God is the one who delights in a ready and willing gift. Paul's contrast in 9:5, between a gift prepared as a blessing and one wrung out grudgingly, shows God's own generous heart, which asks His people to share in His open-handedness and not to resent it. For worship, the passage leads us to see our budgets, accounts and promises as matters that stand before God and that He cares about, and to thank Him for the faithful, unglamorous people who make His work possible.

crossReferences.note: Paul's earlier plan for the collection: the Corinthians choose men they approve, he sends them with letters to carry the gift, and he travels with them only if it is advisable. The delegation here is the working out of that plan, and it shows that Paul was consistent about accountability.

Be careful to do what is right in the eyes of everyone. This is the same idea as 8:21, in almost the same Greek words. It shows that the care for a good name was not a special rule for money but a general duty of believers before a watching world.

Let love and faithfulness not leave you, and you will find favor and a good name in the sight of God and man. Paul's aim in verse 21 draws on this proverb, which joins God's approval and public reputation in one pursuit.

Paul answers the charge that he took advantage of the Corinthians through those he sent, asking whether Titus did and whether they did not walk in the same Spirit. This later passage shows that the care in chapter 8 paid off, and that his critics had in fact been watching the handling of the gift.

The Jerusalem church chose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to oversee the distribution to widows. Here is an earlier case of a church guarding its common funds through trusted, chosen people, which Paul's delegation follows.

A list of Paul's traveling companions from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and Asia. It gives a glimpse of the real party that accompanied the collection and shows that the representatives were drawn from several churches.

Paul tells the Thessalonians that he never used flattery or a pretext for greed, and that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden. It is the same integrity in a personal key and explains why he took such care here.

Epaphroditus, the Philippians' messenger, is called their apostle and minister to Paul's need, and Paul asks that he be honored. It shows another example of a church's messenger, and it shows how highly Paul regarded such servants.
Keep your conduct among the nations honorable so that they may see your good deeds and glorify God. This is the same motive as 8:21, that visible integrity leads outsiders to honor God.

A false scale is an abomination to the LORD, but an accurate weight is His delight. The text is a short statement of what Paul's whole arrangement tries to secure, that those who handle money should handle it honestly, because the LORD cares about such things.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning the Bible shows that people are made to be stewards. In Genesis 1:28 and 2:15 the man and woman are given the earth to rule and to keep, and the fall begins when stewardship turns into grasping. Throughout the story that follows, God keeps asking for faithful stewards and finding few. Joseph manages Egypt's grain and saves many lives, Genesis 41. The tabernacle builders handle the people's gold with accounts that can be checked, Exodus 38. The kings of Israel are told not to multiply silver and gold for themselves, Deuteronomy 17:17, and most of them do.

The prophets then condemn leaders who enrich themselves from the flock, Ezekiel 34:2-4, and promise a shepherd who will feed the sheep with justice. That promise is the background for Jesus, who is the good shepherd and the faithful servant, and who in Luke 12:42 speaks of the wise and faithful steward who gives the household its food at the proper time. The apostle's care for the collection belongs to that chapter in the story. It is the first generation of the church learning to be a trustworthy household.

The passage also looks sideways to the unity of the church. The delegates from several regions are chosen to carry the gift of the nations to the people of Israel, and their journey stitches the two halves of God's family together. Paul calls them messengers of the churches and the glory of Christ, language that lifts a mundane trip into the story of the gospel moving outward from Jerusalem and returning with gifts from the nations, as Isaiah 60:6 and 66:20 had pictured.

The story ends with the account given by every steward, Matthew 25:21, when the faithful hear, 'Well done, good and faithful servant,' and with a city whose gates are never shut and in which nothing impure enters, Revelation 21:25-27. In the new creation there will be no need for audited accounts, because there will be no deceit and no shame. Until then, the church's ordinary honesty with money is a small signpost of that world, and the people who carry gifts faithfully are, in Paul's phrase, the glory of Christ.

quiz.q: Why does Paul give thanks to God concerning Titus?

options.text: Because God put into Titus's heart the same earnest devotion Paul had for the Corinthians.
options.note: Paul credits God for the eager care he found in Titus.

options.text: Because Titus had volunteered to raise the most money.
options.note: The emphasis is on God-given devotion, not fundraising totals.

options.text: Because Titus needed to be persuaded to go.
options.note: Titus came eagerly of his own volition, welcoming the appeal.

options.text: Because Titus had rebuked the Corinthians severely.
options.note: The passage speaks of devotion and eagerness, not rebuke.

quiz.q: Why does Paul take such care in administering the collection?

options.text: To do what is right in the eyes of the Lord and also in the eyes of men, avoiding any criticism.
Because he did not trust the Corinthians at all.
options.note: The concern is integrity in handling funds, not distrust of the givers.

options.text: Because the law required a certain procedure.
options.note: It is gospel integrity, not a legal procedure, that drives him.

options.text: Because he wanted a share of the money for himself.
options.note: Paul guards precisely against any such suspicion.

quiz.q: What does Paul call the brothers sent with the offering?

options.text: Messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
options.note: Verse 23 names them the glory of Christ, displaying His honor.

options.text: Officials appointed by the Roman authorities.
options.note: They were chosen by the churches, not by civil authorities.

options.text: Untested newcomers taking their first assignment.
options.note: They were proven and praised, not untested.

options.text: Paid agents hired to transport funds.
options.note: They are servants of the churches reflecting Christ, not hired agents.

quiz.q: Why does Paul send the brothers ahead before he arrives?

options.text: So the Corinthians would be ready and his boasting about them would not prove empty.
options.note: Verses 3 to 5 give exactly this reason.

options.text: So they could collect the gift by force if needed.
options.note: The gift was to be given willingly, not extracted by force.

options.text: Because he no longer intended to visit himself.
options.note: Paul plans to come, possibly with Macedonians, and wants them ready.

options.text: So the money could be spent before he came.
options.note: The aim was to prepare the gift generously, not to spend it early.

questions: Paul thanks God for the devotion He placed in Titus's heart. How does it change your view of Christian service to see even the willingness to serve as a gift from God?
Paul insisted on doing what is right in the eyes of men as well as the Lord. Where in your life or work does your integrity need to be visible and not merely private?
The brothers are called the glory of Christ because His honor shone through their service. Whose faithful service has shown you something of Christ, and how might yours do the same?
Paul arranged accountability so no one could criticize how the money was handled. How seriously do you take transparency in the way money is handled in the church?
Paul wanted the gift prepared willingly and not begrudgingly. What would it take for your giving to be ready and glad rather than last-minute and reluctant?

translationNotes.note: The gracious offering that we administer refers to the Jerusalem collection; a source footnote points to 1 Corinthians 16:3 to 4 for the parallel arrangements.
Messengers of the churches renders a word that a footnote notes may also be translated apostles, here in the wider sense of sent representatives rather than the twelve apostles.
